articles.title: Protomaps: Self-hosting map tiles has gotten cheap and easy
articles.summary: Protomaps: Self-hosting map tiles has gotten cheap and easy

top_comments: OpenFreeMap is a similar project:https://openfreemap.org/> What is OpenFreeMap?> OpenFreeMap lets you display custom maps on your website and apps for free.> Using our public instance is completely free: there are no limits on the number of map views or requests. There’s no registration, no user database, no API keys, and no cookies. We aim to cover the running costs of our public instance through donations.> What is the tech stack?> There is no tile server running; only nginx serving a Btrfs image with 300 million hard-linked files. This was my idea; I haven’t read about anyone else doing this in production, but it works really well.

We're doing something like this behind Cloudflare R2, same concept of owning the map infra (for privacy and access-control) and reducing load on public infrastructure.If you are into this stuff, you can view PMTiles from the CLI with "gloss", or try to drag-and-drop on its web interface [1]. It seems large tiles (>128M) and some raster formats are failing; plus it would be nice to load from URL there. Will fix that...(AI warning). ntmaps [2] is a Golang library that lets you use different tile providers, deployable in terminal or browser. ntplaygrounds [3] uses that and nt3d and ntactor to make a city simulation. Data is pulled from OpenStreetMap in those.[1] https://nimbleterminal.com/gloss/app.html [2] https://nimbleterminal.com/ntmaps [3] https://nimbleterminal.com/ntplaygrounds

yeah, basemaps are small enough to store and host cost effectively, but high res satellite imagery gets big and expensive fast as you go up in zoom level. I built my own satellite mosaic of North America for my app so I can offer users offline access to the tiles and had to stop at z17 because of projected storage requirements. high res global coverage can get you into the hundreds of TB range which is no longer in the "stick it on r2 and serve it with a worker" or "download and upload the entire dataset sequentially over your residential internet" territorythe fun/hard parts of the project weren't really scale dependent, although downloading source imagery and building the tile pyramids did take literally weeks to run. actually, the hardest part was getting demosaicing right, e.g. making the quilt seamless. filtering out cloudy and smokey/hazy tiles while picking alternatives from the same time of year so groundcover & crops are in a consistent growth stage so you don't end up with checkerboard patterns or cloud silhouettes randomly across your map. and there were other problems that came up more or less just because of how & when the satellite took the images that require exposure correction and more filteringI also have a pelias index with 170M records for search and self-host valhalla for routing. the open source mapping ecosystem has really impressed me the more I learn with each project

articles.title: Old Bitly links are being hijacked
articles.summary: Old Bitly links are being hijacked

top_comments: Link shorteners that are outsourced are in my humble opinion an order of magnitude worse for the internet than they would be if in-house.The way they accrete URLs over time, and then time passes, and anything can happen (your account gets deactivated, shortener company goes out of business / experiences catastrophic data loss / etc) is just asking for permanently broken links which may be unfixable.Especially when you consider how these services can, unless they're spammy enough to inject gross interstitial ad pages, make 0 revenue from you if you aren't currently paying for a premium service, it's easy to see how they can go under.Note: Clearly with the kind of ephemeral crap these 2011 tweets were, I'm assuming the 'attacker' publicized "Hey guys look at these funny tweets" because obviously who cares about 15 year old McDonalds marketing messages. But in general it's sad to see these still being used. To be fair to bitly, they do offer the ability to use your own domain at least, but sadly, with a service targeted mainly at marketing departments, usually they don't have the ability to work with the in-house tech team(s) to even set up DNS.

Short anecdote: Famous author (with huge fanbase!) used a Bit.ly link in one of their books (the narrative needed a fake tweet with fake link). Editor didn't notice/care and never registered it. I noticed on release date, caught it and redirected it to a website that referenced the book, a few people tweet about it thinking the author used the link on purpose!
I think the biggest surprise to me is that a URL shortener makes enough money to have a Trust and Safety team. I assumed it was just a side project a person or two ran.

What made Steve Jobs great was that he would rather have Apple cannibalize its successful product lines than fall prey to a competitor. You can see this pattern with the iPod. The iPod disrupted itself many, many times. The iPod Mini then the iPod Nano. Then the iPod shuffle as the answer to the race ot the bottom.The biggest moment was partnering with Motorola as phones started becoming more capable and flash memory got cheaper to bring music to phones, which was then the prelude to the iPhone.The iPhone killed the iPod. Most companies would have never created the product, because it would have killed their golden goose, but Jobs did.Just like he went all in on the iPad which had the potential to kill the cheap student Mac.If Nvidia's next CEO is smart, they'd buy up a bunch of these companies that "burn" weights to silicon, make the process better, and then sell that as a service. Let it cannibalize the sales of their products. It's better for them to do it to themselves than their competitors.

As the author mentions, the biggest threat is from customers becoming competitors. The problem space is stabilizing and this allows the biggest buyers of GPUs to work with companies like broadcom to make their own chips. Thanks to agents, they can also spin up their own abstraction layers and debug tools. CUDA is becoming less relevant, and the rate at which that is happening is about to go parabolic.Surely Nvidia won’t stand still and will continue to compete, but the margins will collapse along with volumes.AMD will probably suffer less, relatively speaking. Their failure to invest in software finally seems to be paying off now that LLMs can pick up their slack. But the growth currently priced in to their stock will never materialize and they’ll be seen as arriving just in time for the lights to go out.
